value.overview: The Violet-headed Hummingbird (Klais guimeti) is a small, compact hummingbird of humid forests, foothills, and forest edges from Central America to northern and western South America. Males are striking, with an iridescent violet-blue crown and throat, while females are duller and more gray below. It is the only species in the genus Klais. Although local in distribution, it may visit gardens, flowering shrubs, and shade-grown agricultural areas within suitable habitat.
value.classification: The Violet-headed Hummingbird belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the order Apodiformes. Klais guimeti is the only species in the genus Klais.
value.identification: This is a tiny, short-billed hummingbird with a relatively compact body and a habit of holding the tail slightly cocked. Adult males have a bright violet to violet-blue crown and throat, green upperparts, and paler grayish underparts. Females have a less vivid bluish crown, a gray throat and underparts, and green upperparts. Both sexes show a noticeable white spot behind the eye. Sex, lighting, and molt can affect the apparent intensity of the head coloration.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Honduras and Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama, then across parts of northern South America, including Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, and adjacent regions. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, occurring mainly in humid lowlands, foothills, and lower mountain habitats, including the Caribbean and southern Pacific regions. It uses edges of humid primary forest, secondary growth, clearings, thickets, gardens, flowering hedges, and other lightly modified habitats. Reported Costa Rican elevations extend from lowlands into foothill areas.
value.migrationStatus: Violet-headed Hummingbirds are generally resident rather than long-distance migrants. In Costa Rica, the species is considered a resident bird and may move locally in response to flowering and changing food availability.
value.breeding: The female is expected to build the nest and provide nearly all parental care, as is typical of hummingbirds. The nest is a very small, open cup made from fine plant fibers and other soft materials, often attached to a slender branch or supported by vegetation. A clutch usually consists of two small white eggs, which the female incubates. Breeding timing can vary geographically and may be associated with local rainfall and periods of abundant flowering.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists primarily of nectar from small flowers, especially those in forest edges, shrubs, thickets, gardens, and other open habitats. The bird also captures small insects and other arthropods, which provide essential protein, particularly during breeding. It may defend productive flowers or feeding patches from other hummingbirds, but its feeding range and territorial behavior can vary with flower abundance and competition.
value.behavior: The Violet-headed Hummingbird is active and agile, making rapid flights between flowers and perches. It commonly forages in low vegetation, shrubbery, forest openings, and edge habitats, and it may visit flowering plants and feeders. Short, direct flights are often interspersed with brief perching periods. Males may display the violet head and throat during encounters with rivals or potential mates. The species can be inconspicuous despite its bright plumage because of its small size and quick movements.

conservation.populationTrend: No reliable evidence of a major global population decline is established, although population estimates and trends are limited in some parts of the range.
